I take advantage of the
presence of the Prime Minister to make a few observations When the Minister of Finance introduced his budget I naturally assumed, with regard to what he said about the stabilization fund, and I think every other member did the same, that it would be promulgated by legislation during the passage of which we might have a general discussion of the whole matter. I find now, from what took place last evening, that the fund is going to be organized and administered under this relief act, and therefore there may be no special legislation introduced in connection with it. Consequently this is the only opportunity we shall have to discuss it. We might discuss the subject on going into supply, but any debate that might take place then would have to be confined to general principles and one could not ask any questions of the minister. It is one thing to have the precise language of a statute and quite another thing to have the more or less general terms which the Minister of Finance used in speaking of his policy with regard to the stabilization fund. I should like to get some definite advice as to just how far this goes.
The Prime Minister last night, speaking of course from memory, said he thought the words fish and fish products were the words
used in connection with fish. That of course is a mistake, because the words used are fresh fish and canned fish. If the right lion, gentleman is in a position to say that he intends it to mean fish and fish products, then what I have to say is practically at an end, and it will be a source of gratification to us in British Columbia.
I wish to plead particularly for an industry that exists solely in the district I represent; that is, the reducing or processing of pilchards. They make pilchard meal and pilchard oil and I do not think there is any other district in Canada where this business is carried on. This industry came into existence-I speak from memory-six or seven years ago, and at that time it was confined entirely to white men, something which is true of very few of the fishing industries in the west. There was a large outlay of capital. There were at one time, if I remember rightly, twenty-seven reduction plants on the west coast of Vancouver island, each with a capital investment of from 85,000 to $8,000. They would each employ perhaps one hundred men, between the men on the plant and the men engaged in catching the fish. That would mean a total employment of some three thousand people, and then as a side line, depending on this, there would be employment for perhaps another five hundred. Owing to the distressed market conditions, instead of twenty-seven stations as there were a few years ago, last year there were, I think, only three in operation. I think they were run more with the idea of relieving the un-emploj'ment situation than with any hope of making a profit, in fact I think that they ended up in the red. This industry could provide employment for a large number of white men, at least it used to provide employment for white men before the British Columbia government fell heir to certain jurisdiction, after which they permitted orientals also to be employed. The cost to the government would be comparatively small but the employment would be quite large. I ask if the government could see its way clear to include pilchard oil and pilchard meal within the terms of the stabilization fund? I received a wire the other day from one of the largest operators. They state that they are disappointed that these commodities have not been included. They told Doctor Found, the Deputy Minister of Fisheries, when he was out there last December, that it was impossible to carry on the reduction industry unless either the cost could be cut or a subsidy provided. They then go on
Relief Act, 1933

to point out that a sales tax has been placed upon fuel oil which adds very considerably to their working expenses and makes it all the more necessary that they should come under this stabilization scheme. The telegram continues :
Would ask your earnest endeavour secure inclusion fish oils under stabilization plan particularly as without some such help the industry must be further curtailed whereas by inclusion we can reasonably look to increased operations and improved employment.
Would the Prime Minister be kind enough to state what his attitude will be in regard to this matter?

I was very much
interested in the Prime Minister's explanation last night as to why certain commodities were put upon the preferred list so far as the adverse exchange on the British market is concerned. speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext:
I think the hon. gentleman is aware of the fact that the production of butter in Canada barely meets the consumption; there is a very small available exportable surplus. This is a relief measure and the evidence which the government had before it was not sufficient to warrant action being taken with respect to butter similar to that taken with respect to cheese, for instance. As a matter of fact, butter is selling at a higher price upon the Canadian market than that prevailing upon any other market of which I know. At the moment the Canadian price is much higher than the British or American prices. In fact, it has been so attractive that our friends in New Zealand have endeavoured to secure this market.
Mr. MOTHERWELL; The dairy industry will be upon an export basis as soon as the full flush of milk comes in the summer. It has been usual for this industry in the past half century to go on an export basis around the first of June in each year. It is usually off the export market in the winter but on in the summer. What will happen after June 1? Unless something happens, I anticipate that the price will be lower than it ever was during the first quarter of this century. That is whiat the present indications point to. This will happen within two or three months, possibly before this house prorogues, and that commodity should be put in a position to take advantage of this intended exchange benefit. This government should be the last to turn a cold shoulder to butter because it owes its position of power in this house largely to the import of butter problem and the export of whiskey. From a sense of gratitude, this commodity should not foe overlooked by my right hon. friend.

I do not know if this is one of the ways adopted for avoiding proper expenditure during the year or for the government to make a better financial showing, but three months is entirely too long for a retailer to wait who has been taking scrip in exchange for goods. There is not a single retailer or merchant who should have to wait that long for payment of his goods.

The minister knows that the wholesale houses will not sell goods on terms of three months, and I believe it is within both the jurisdiction of the minister and of the provincial government to see that these bills are paid more promptly. I should like to propose an amendment to section 9, as follows:
That section 9 be amended by adding the following words thereto: "Provided also that subsection (b) of section 2 shall be inoperative during the time parliament is in session."
Subsection (b) of section 2 reads as follows:
Notwithstanding the provisions of any statute or law the governor in council may:
(b) Take all such measures as in his discretion may be deemed necessary or advisable to maintain, within the competence of parliament, peace, order and good government throughout Canada, and to protect the credit and financial position of the dominion or any province thereof.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that unless this section is amended in the way I have indicated we will be in the anomalous position that even while parliament may be sitting and may be enacting laws deemed to be necessary by the peoples' representatives the governor in council may overrule and override any law which parliament may pass.
I think if we in this House of Commons, as legislators, are to be asked to commit hara-kiri, we ought to have, at least, one clause which will help to save our faces during the time parliament is in session. The purport of the amendment is to ensure that at least for the time that parliament is actually in session it will be supreme in the matter of any enactment which may be necessary for the purpose of maintaining within the competence of parliament peace, order and good government throughout Canada. speechtext: The house resumed from Tuesday, March 21, consideration of the motion of Hon. E. N. Rhodes (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a fellow Nova
Scotian it is to me always a pleasure to listen to my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes). His long parliamentary experience, his knowledge of public affairs and his voice and pleasing presence makes it a matter of gratification to hear him sjpeak on almost any subject. Last year I had the pleasure of congratulating him upon his accession to the honourable post of Minister of Finance of the Dominion of Canada, and I was at least able to congratulate him upon his manner of presentation and the distinction he had received even though I could not go far in congratulating him upon the tenor of the budget speech which he delivered.
My hon. friend, after one year, has had experience which I am sure must lead him to realize that there are onerous as well as honourable duties in connection with the Department of Finance. When listening to him the other day, knowing the outstanding position he occupies among his colleagues, I could not help thinking that if this was the best my hon. friend could do in the way of a budget surely this country is far from well off under the government which at present sits opposite.
In discussing the budget to-day the question which I put to myself and to the house is this: Will this be the budget when we get through with it in this house? I recollect that in years gone by, while my right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) was Minister of Finance, budgets were brought in which indicated that the main policy of this government was one of being able to right about face should the exigency require, and I shall be very much surprised if some of the

terms of this budget are not dropped before this session is over. I do not know of any government in Canada since 1867 which has shown the ability to start and stop as readily as this government has. I remember that my right hon. friend the Prime Minister announced in no uncertain terms that we were to have sound money in this country, and he decried the use of the printing press. It was not so many weeks after he made that statement in this house and on the platforms of this country, however, that he put through the neatest little bit of inflation with printing press currency that we know of anywhere, in the issue of $35,000,000 of Dominion notes. How was that money secured? It was secured by treasury bills which the government first gave to the banks in order to secure a loan from the banks to the government; the banks then promptly handed back the government's own treasury bills and got $35,000,000 in Dominion notes for them.
I mention this instance to indicate that one cannot be certain that the assurances one may receive from the treasury benches, even from the right hon. Prime Minister, will verily come to pass. There are other instances I might mention. I remember distinctly that in one budget introduced by my right hon. friend the Prime Minister there was a headliner by way of an amendment to the Income Tax Act, but we all know what happened. It fell by the wayside; it never was put through. There was a tax on cheques under $5 which was abandoned, and certain exemptions under the sales tax which were to be struck out were left in. In introducing that budget my right hon. friend had the opportunity of his life to carry out the idea which he had so strenuously advocated and so forcibly expressed when he was on this side of the house, that is, to conscript portions of the deposits in banks and the insurance companies, but nothing whatever, was' heard of that proposal. Finally, in connection with that budget I remember my right hon. friend singing his swan song as Minister of Finance and expressing the regret he felt that he had been unable to carry out those policies which were so near and dear to his heart. Here is what he said, as it appears at page 3307 of Hansard for July 2, 1931:
I believe my hon. friend from Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) was sincere in his suggestion with regard to taxation, beoause on more than one occasion he has done me the honour to talk about the matter privately. Probably he will realize that the disappointment to me is far greater than it can be to him and in fact greater to me than to any other hon. member. Realizing those facts he will appreciate my position. I should like to have seen applied in Canada some new system of taxation, and

The Budget-Mr. Ralston
he is quite right when he says it is not at all probable that I shall ever have a chance to try a new form of taxation, because it is not at all likely that 1 shall ever again submit ways and means to this house. I am not without hope, however, that some Minister of Finance-
I commend this to my hon. friend who now occupies that portfolio.
-reviewing the means by which taxes may be raised will realize the values and benefits accruing from a turnover tax.
Then he went on to say:
Sir, it has not been my privilege to introduce any new forms of taxation to this country at this time.
If he has not introduced new qualities certainly he has introduced them in quanti

ties; there is no doubt about that.
I do not for a single moment disguise the fact that I would like to have done so. I should like to have written a budget which would have expressed my views -with respect to taxation in Canada. That privilege has not been given, and it never will be.
And women wept and strong men bowed their heads. Then we had the spectacle just last fall of my right hon. friend rising in his place and intimating, if ever a Prime Minister intimated anything, that there was to be a measure brought down providing for unemployment insurance, that the matter had been considered and was to be placed before the Dominion-provincial conference, and that there were indications that it would go through. That made splendid newspaper publicity, but once more the constitution, my right hon. friend's bulwark, got in the way and as a result unemployment insurance is not to be introduced. Why? Because the provinces do not want it he says.
What I want to know is whether the government will stick to this budget or whether, when one speaks about it, he will be speaking about something which will be discarded before the budget is finally adopted.
There are some things that are sure, however, and of those things I want to speak first. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance has had a good many weeks to consider this budget. It was coming down the first week in March; then, due to events which were taking place south of the line, it was delayed. Naturally I have not had the opportunity which the minister has had to consider the various subjects dealt with in the budget, and therefore of course my treatment of them must be cursory as compared to his- and I mean cursory in the strict grammatical sense of the word rather than what it sounds like. There is one point I should like to mention, however, in dealing 53719-213
with the matter of time; I feel that I should put it on record. I am sorry that the Prime Minister is not in his place. Were it only a personal matter I would not mention it, but I think it has to do with the usual procedure of parliament and with the practice which has been long established in connection with the reply to the budget. The right hon. gentleman the other evening, in replying to my right hon. leader, intimated that a somewhat longer time than usual was being given to the representative of the opposition who had moved the adjournment of this debate-I presume he referred to myself. I have looked up Hansard and I find that when my hon. friend the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) was to reply to the budget he had four days. I find that when the present Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan) replied to the budget he had four days. I find that when the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) replied to the budget, when he was leader of the opposition in 1930, he had five days. I have been given three days. I just put that on record so that my right hon. friend-

As I have said there are some things in this budget which will not be changed and of which one can be sure regardless of what may take place in relation to the proposals contained in the budget. The Minister of Finance comes into this house representing, let us say, the board of directors of Canada Incorporated, and making his report upon the fiscal administration for the year. He is asked immediately, and he asks himself in making his report:	How about what the Prime
Minister calls the equilibrium between revenue and expenditure-has that been maintained? What is his answer? His answer is that unfortunately the equilibrium has not been maintained, but that there is a deficit on ordinary account of $53,000,000. Someone speaks up and says: Is that all? He says: No, that is not all. In addition to that there are special expenditures, less special revenues, of $38,000,000; capital expenditures of $9,000,000; loans and non-active advances of $2,000,000, making a total of $102,000,000 short of the amount of revenue collected. country to extract from them each year these increasingly large sums of money and make no provision for the retirement of our national obligations. The sum to be set aside is not large. I can only say this, that if we on this side of the house were entrusted with power, we would not hesitate a single moment to make provision for the retirement of the national debt of this country.
Since that was paid, $445,000,000 have been added to the public debt of this country and not only has not one dollar been set aside to take care of that debt but there will be another deficit of $90,000,000 this year even though we balance the ordinary expenditure and raise all the money my hon. friend expects to raise by taxation. They have also entered into a guarantee with regard to the marketing of the 1930 wheat crop. I do not intend to spend much time on that subject this afternoon, but it is being discussed in the public press of the country. While I am prepared to admit that the Prime Minister did not deliberately mean to mislead the house, he certainly left an impression which was different from the facts with regard to the marketing of the 1930 wheat crop and the guarantee

The Budget-Mr. Ralston
that was given. He left on the house the impression that the operations which were being conducted by Mr. McFarland were in connection with the wheat which was being taken over from the farmers. Instead of that, what was done, as I am informed, was this: they took the wheat purchased from the farmer and converted it into "futures" from time to time. This may or may not have been good policy, because it was betting against the future, but it had this in its favour, that the "futures" represented wheat actually purchased from the farmer, and it might be legitimately a matter which the government might, to save carrying charges, turn over and over in the hope that a loss might eventually be saved. But I say it is absolutely wrong for the government to guarantee that marketing operation and permit it not simply to deal in wheat purchased from the farmer but to speculate in futures which have nothing to do with the wheat purchased from the farmer originally, and to do this in order to accomplish two objects: first to bolster up the market, that is, Mr. McFarland or his agency, having attempted to sell find the market low, and adopt the simple expedient of themselves buying "futures" in order to create a demand. That is the way they bolster up the market. Secondly, faced with a situation where there is a drop in the "futures" which they hold, they go into the market, but not simply to handle the same quantity of wheat they had before, but to speculate and to cover their loss by making a bet in July for instance that the price of wheat in October, say, will have gone up by that time, and they buy more wheat in the form of futures. While my right hon. friend (Mr. Bennett) calls it hedging, it is no more hedging than it is for me, if I am in the market holding Montreal Light, Heat and Power and find it going down, to go and buy Consolidated Gas to endeavour to recover my losses. That is not hedging at all. It is just plain, ordinary speculation, or what is more properly called gambling in the wheat market. My hon. friend and the government have backed up an organization which is doing that. They say it is in the interests of the western farmers. I say that they should cut their loss in connection with the respectable transaction of buying the farmer's wheat and should not keep on trading back and forth, in "futures" transactions that have nothing whatever to do with the quantity of wheat that has been purchased from the farmers themselves. My *hon. friend the Minister of Finance last year gave us the IMr. Ralston.]
impression that there was going to be no loss from that operation. Let me read what he said, at page 1759 of Hansard of 1932:
The house will recall the problems which the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, faced in financing its operations in connection with the 1930 crop. The government, believing that it was in the national interest to protect the credit of the marketing agencies in such a way that the grain might be marketed to the general advantage of growers, had given an undertaking to the seven chartered banks concerned, which then made available the necessary credits. The undertaking was given status by order in council P.C. 2238, dated September 12, 1931. This undertaking-
This was in the budget speech of a year ago:

has served its purpose, and without cost to the treasury. Based upon present market prices the expectation is that, when all accounts are settled, the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, will be able -to settle all advances without recourse being had to the dominion's guarantee.
Even if that had been so, it is no justification for this government going into wheat speculation with the money of the people of Canada. Let me go further and give the statement of my right hon. friend the Prime Minister last fall, at page 1093 of Hansard. He is speaking of the different people who are in the grain business, and he says that the second class, the speculator, has disappeared, and he gave the impression that the government had taken the speculator's place. He said:
Under these circumstances, Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers Limited, to which I have referred, became the only available hedging organization left in western Canada, and the government is faced at the moment with the issue as to whether or not, under these circumstances, it would give its support as provided by the Relief Act passed in 1931 and 1932 as well-this being a product of the field and the farm,-by guaranteeing to the banks such sums as might be necessary to enable these operations to be carried on by this organization. But before that was done the government had to consider whether or not the interest of Canada as a whole would be best served by continuing the bonus which we granted last year or by taking the steps I have just indicated for the purpose of protecting the general situation in connection with the marketing of wheat.
That is where my right hon. friend, perhaps unconsciously, misleads people. He says that it is done to protect the general situation. What that means in plain, ordinary language is that they were buying wheat in addition to what was purchased from the farmers in order to support the market, in the hope that some day the price of wheat would go up. It is exactly as the farm loan board did in the United

The Budget-Mr. Ralston
States, with this exception, that this organization in this country goes further and trades in wheat "futures" that do not at all represent what has been taken over physically. The Prime Minister went on:
I hasten to assure the house that on a balance of financial benefits it is clear that in respect of any Obligations which might be incurred-it is not possible that any heavy obligations [DOT] will be incurred unless something very unforeseen happens-the amount involved *will be less than would be involved by the payment of the bonus requested. Weighing the situation as a whole, the probabilities pro and con, the effect upon the dominion, the business which would be secured and the chaos which would result from the absolute failure to sell wheat except as a distress commodity, the steps which I have indicated were taken.
If I might say so, I do not think any good purpose would be served by going into the details of the operations which we have entrusted to the organizations I have mentioned under the management of Mr. McFarland. However, the closest supervision has been exercised and we believe and we have had no reason to change our minds at the present moment, that the steps taken will be more beneficial to the dominion as a whole and will secure for the country as a whole greater advantages than if we paid the producer the bonus which was paid last year and which we are pressed to continue this year. Except for the mention of the exact financial amount involved, which obviously it is difficult to give, I think I have answered all the questions asked.
Those are the Prime Minister's words. Now what was said in the budget speech of 1933? Last year there was going to be no financial commitment. What does the Minister of Finance say this year? At page 3220 of Hansard he says:
The guarantee of advances to Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers Limited in connection with the 1930 crop remains in effect, and it was necessary during the past season for the company to increase its liability as a result of stabilizing transactions which it was considered expedient in the public interest to support. To these operations the government gave its guarantee. The steadiness which has developed in the wheat market has undoubtedly vindicated the action then taken-
Note this:
-and the question of ultimate liability will depend entirely upon the future course of wheat prices.
How naive! 'Could it be anything else but that? Of course it will depend on future prices. How much had the government's action to do with stabilizing the wheat situation? On account of the situation in the United States recently there was a flurry in wheat in Winnipeg and the market went up. I do not think the government's action had a great deal to do with that. It may be that my right hon. friend may pull out of this transaction with a whole skin, and certainly
everybody hopes he will, but it will not be because of his business administration but simply because he happened to be lucky, just the same as I might be if, having purchased a ticket on the Calcutta sweepstake, I drew the grand prize. That was done under the Unemployment Relief Act. I need not say what everyone realizes-uny hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) himself pointed it out in a speech not long ago, how important the wheat market is to this country that .our farmers should sell their wheat, but our farmers themselves I am sure do not want this government to go into gambling in wheat to support the market, and the government should take its loss and get out and be rid of that transaction.
With regard to relief moneys generally, there has been a good deal said in the debates which have just closed, and in previous years, with regard to the expenditures. I believe it will be found that there has been absolutely no considered, deliberate policy with regard to relief. When our descendants, supposing they enter a time of stress and strain, which God forbid, such as we have had, look back and find out how we handled unemployment, I do not believe they will be able to find very much light in the darkness in order to guide them in evolving a policy in that respect. They will find that we spent money, and spent it lavishly, but they will not find any enlistment whatever of national effort; they will not find any national organization. They will find a blanket vote, money paid out for this, that and the other, and guarantees on all sides. But they will find no deliberate, ordered policy in connection with this great question of unemployment.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that they will find that what happened was this: We started out with a vote of $20,000,000, which was supposed to be in part for public works and part for direct relief. They will find that we got into public works and that we forced on the provinces and the municipalities in this dominion an expenditure of $100,000,000, which is a noose around their necks to-day. Now we have come back again to direct relief because, forsooth, of constitutional difficulties. That is going to be the record which is going to be read by our descendants when the time comes for them to look over what we have done and the policy that we have adopted in connection with relief.
With regard to other expenditures, on the Canadian National Railways, my right hon. friend the Prime Minister, speaking at Hamilton a short time ago-I have not the speech
The Budget-Mr. Ralston

here but I read it Last night-indicated in no uncertain terms that it was the Liberal party which 'built and guaranteed two transcontinental railways and set them out to compete with one another. My right hon. friend, if he knows anything at all, knows the history of those roads. He knows that the Grand Trunk Pacific and the National Transcontinental were voted for in 1904, and that the building was commenced at that time. He knows that at that time there was a policy on the part of the Conservative party for a second transcontinental railroad, except that it was to take the form of completing the existing railroad to the coast. He knows, further than that, that in 1911 the Liberal government refused a grant to extend the Canadian Northern to the Pacific coast and in 1912 the first vote was made by the government he supported, a vote of $6,000,000 to extend the Canadian Northern railway through the Yellowhead pass to Vancouver; and he knows that not until 1914 was the large grant made of $45,000,000 in order to make the Canadian Northern a transcontinental railway with a terminus on the Pacific coast as stated by Sir Robert Borden at that time. That is the early history of the railroads.
He knows that in 1917 there was an opportunity to take over those roads as bankrupt concerns. He knows that instead of that $10,800,000 was paid for the stock of the Canadian Northern railroad, that we took the railroad over, and that we have its bonds to-day. He knows the Grand Trunk was taken over also by the Meighen government, and at that time, after arbitration, although nothing was paid for the stock the bonds were assumed, because we took the road. There was no attempt made to write down the bonds, but operation was taken over and, as the Duff report states, in 1917, government ownership of the railroads was adopted.
Yet at Hamilton my right hon. friend stated it was the Liberal party which built two transcontinental railroads and set them to compete with one another.

The Gibb report is mentioned also as perhaps giving some promise of a reduction in expenses. The Minister of Finance had hardly said his last word before the right hon. Prime Minister rose in his place and indicated that because of representations that had been received from various quarters it was doubtful whether the legislation based on the Gibb report would be brought down. So I say it is very difficult for one to tell exactly whether this will be the budget we will finally consider.
Now let me mention one or two other matters that are in the minds of the people, though hon. gentlemen opposite may say they are minor matters. I imagine there were very few people in this country, when they saw the contents of this budget, with the taxes which are being imposed and the lack of any real reduction in expenditure, who did not immediately think of the radio commission, for which we are being asked to vote 81,000,000 at a time like this. I think the very first day the estimates of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) were brought down I took occasion to say a word with regard to a salary which was being increased in his department. That salary is being paid to a man who I understand is a returned soldier and who, I understand, is in every way well equipped for his job. It did seem to me, however, that it indicated an attitude of mind on the part of the government which they should not have at this time; it seemed to me they had not gone over the estimates and pruned them as they should have. I remember a research item of $21,000, I think in the estimates of the Minister of Trade and Commerce again, which could have been cut out just as well as not. It was there as usual; we were asked to vote it as usual. Apparently no real consideration has been given by the government to the question of really pruning these estimates and cutting the coat to fit the cloth. These are matters the people of this country have in mind at this time; these are matters which are going to cause more of an uproar than there already has been if some real attempt is not made by the government to reduce expenditure.
On the other side of the picture the income tax is to be increased, not in the way that was proposed by the right hon. Prime Minister two years ago but at least to some extent. Here again the small taxpayer is being brought in; exemptions are being lowered and there is to be an increase of 650 per cent imposed
[Mr. Ralston. 1
on the man earning a salary of $2,500, with only a 14 per cent increase imposed on the man with an income of $50,000. Those are matters about which the people are wondering. I do not think any more illuminating document could have been published-and I say this to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Ryckman), who is not in his seat-than the chart which recently appeared in the National Revenue Review, which shows the collections Of income tax from certain classes of the community, and in certain income brackets. I say that publications such as this give information a great deal more quickly than long rows of figures, and I want to congratulate the minister on having published this statement.
I have no doubt the income tax will bring in a large amount of money; at least I hope it will, but at the same time I believe in his own heart the Minister of Finance is convinced that he is making a mistake in going to perhaps ten thousand, fifteen thousand or twenty thousand people and getting small contributions of $2, $5 or $10. I believe the cost of collection will almost equal the amount of money he collects. Perhaps this is being done with the idea of equality of sacrifice, but if all this time my right hon. friend has left out this class I do not think that when he brings them in he should at the same time increase the tax on small incomes so greatly while the tax on an income of $50,000 is increased by only 14 per cent. I shall not deal at greater length with matters of income tax generally, because they can be discussed later on when the bill is brought down.
Let us consider for a moment the other taxes. There is to be a tax of two cents per pound on sugar, and I understand that molasses is taken from the exempted list under the sales tax. We are told that $20,000,000 is expected to be raised from the tax on sugar. That amounts to $2 per head for every man, woman and child in this dominion and I submit, Mr. Speaker, that this tax, bearing as it does upon a necessity of life that always has been regarded as an essential, coupled with the removal of molasses from the list of exempted goods under the sales tax, imposes a very great hardship on the poorer people of this dominion. So far as the sugar industry is concerned I have no fault to find with my hon. friend. That industry is well protected; in fact it is too well protected, but this tax is not going to be paid by the sugar industry. This tax of two cents a pound will be paid by the individual householder who, with sugar at the present price, will have to pay a 50 per cent tax on all the sugar going into his house.
The removal of other foodstuffs from exemption under the sale tax will bring about the

The Budget-Mr. Ralston
same result. I have not gone over the list of exemptions carefully enough to know how many commodities are included, but I do know that generally speaking it is foodstuffs that are affected.
Then we come to the nuisance taxes, and first there is the tax on cheques under $5. Two years ago the Prime Minister abandoned that idea, but now he takes it up again. With regard to the tax on bonds and on payments made out of Canada I have no doubt that my right hon. friend has received representations long before this from companies all over this dominion who have had their corporation tax increased by one and a half per cent and who now will be forced in addition to absorb this tax on interest payable in the United States. Why do I say that? Because of the fact that the trust deeds, in almost every case, under which bonds are issued provide that the company must absorb any tax that may be levied except Canadian income tax, and as a result instead of taxing the foreigner receiving this bond interest my hon. friend is taxing the Canadian company. As I say, I have no doubt that representations have been received by my hon. friend the Minister of Finance before this, and if he has received telegrams similar to those I have received I have no doubt he will have to give serious consideration to this further taxation of Canadian companies.
With regard to the taxation of foreign investments in this country, the Prime Minister knows the argument that was advanced two years ago as to foreign capital coming to Canada. He knows whether or not that argument is effective; he knows far better than I do. Two years ago the Prime Minister abandoned this tax after it was proposed. Whether he will do the same thing now remains to be seen. I do point out to him, however, that this is a debtor and not a creditor country, that we are a borrowing and not a lending nation, and any tax on capital coming here to help our industrial development must be considered very carefully. With regard t-o taxation generally, however, I have no doubt my right hon. friend is saying that the opposition have nothing to do with taxation anyway. This is what he said in 1928:
There is not much to he gained by an opposition suggesting anything with respert to the income tax nor indeed, for that matter, respecting taxation generally. Taxes must be imposed by the government and under our institutions proposals in this regard must originate with the administration of the day. The government only can take the necessary action in this respect.
My right hon. friend has made the proposals, but I miss my guess very much if those proposals are not considerably changed before this bill gets out of the committee of ways and means.
My hon. friend, as one headliner in the budget, indicates that he is going to establish what he calls a stabilization fund. Stabilization is a better word than bonus-agricultural stabilization. It means, according to the hon. gentleman, that there is to be paid to the exporter of certain products which are named in the budget the difference between the current rate of exchange and $4.60 in connection with goods shipped to Great Britain.
Now, no one can tell how it is going to work out until he sees the result next year.
I said the same thing about the wheat bonus and I repeat it now in regard to this matter. In principle I am opposed to this sort of legislation, because I do not believe it is sound but if bonuses are going they ought to extend to every natural product and, as someone suggests, factory products as well.
I cannot see how you can pick out some part of the community shipping to Great Britain and say to that class that they will have a certain amount made up on what they lose in shipping to Great Britain, while other exporters are given no such consideration. Take for instance the fresh fish producers. According to this they will get a bonus, but the preserved fish man does not. Why, I cannot understand. Again, the canned fish man receives consideration, but the man whose product is pickled fish does not. I have no idea what the reason for this discrimination can be. Take lumber, coal, wheat -they are left out altogether; and the same applies to butter, apples and all these other products. W'hat the reason is, we do not know. One could name numbers of natural products that fall into the same category. After all, Mr. Speaker, I ask you: Is there any guarantee, except what the Prime Minister said last evening to the effect that the government were considering the matter of machinery, that the man who actually produces the goods will get the benefit of this bonus? The exporter is the one who will get it, according to the budget speech. Is this going to be the practical working out of it- that perhaps the people of this country are to pay S2 per head of a tax on sugar in order to subsidize the British consumer? Is that going to be the practical outcome? The benefit may never accrue at all to our producer, because this is a buyer's market. The buyer may say to him, "Yes, but you are getting so much from the government and you must take that off the price." The result is that the British consumer will get his goods that much lower. How is the Prime Minister going to prevent it? I hope he has in mind some means whereby he can prevent this
The Budget-Mr. Ralston

occurring, but I would point out that very often schemes of this kind miscarry. My right hon. friend has to watch two individuals in connection with such a scheme-not only the British consumer but the exporter as well.
Let me make a few observations with regard to fish. I say to my hon. friend that he will not get very far in assisting the fishermen of the east in shipping fresh fish to England. I believe there was about $300,000 worth of fresh fish shipped last year to England whereas the shipments to the United States amounted to something like $6,000,000. If this provision is intended to assist the producer of fish, why does he not get the bonus for the fish he ships to the United States as well as to Great Britain? What is the difference? He ships $300,000 worth to one market and $6,000,000 to the other. I am afraid this will not do our Atlantic coast fishermen any good. I shall be very glad to see them get it, and I advocated it when the wheat bonus was brought up. But the fact is that you will not find any large shipment of fresh fish to Great Britain.
I say to the Minister of Finance, who was formerly Minister of Fisheries, that if he wishes to help the shore fishermen of the maritime provinces all he has to do is to refuse licences to trawlers when they expire on March 31. That would be more helpful to that class of the community than this stabilization fund can possibly prove. I say that to the minister in all seriousness. I mentioned this last fall, and now is the time to aot. The provision of the order in council is to the effect that if the shore fishermen can supply the market then the trawler licences are not to be granted, and I say that the time has come when trawler licences should be refused, inasmuch as the shore . fishermen are in a position to supply more than the market which they have. Moreover, the price is only about three-quarters of a cent per pound and at that figure they can hardly make a living wage; they must have the maximum of production to make even a fair portion of a day's wage. Last fall I put on record the receipts of the fishermen from day to day, and the situation revealed then has not shown any improvement. I say to my hon. friend therefore that he would do far more for the shore fishermen by refusing licences to trawlers off the Nova Scotia coast than he can possibly do in connection with the stabilization fund.
_ This idea of trying to assist an industry by simply having one part of the community 
contribute to another seption is something I do not agree with. We are not getting anywhere by pursuing that policy; we are simply lifting ourselves by our bootstraps. That, I submit, is not the sort of policy that will revive trade and produce tonnage for our railways and revenues through the Customs department. It cannot be done that way. We must find some means whereby exports will be encouraged and revenues will be obtained, not through increased prices to be charged the people of Canada but from the people who are buying in the markets of the world.

An average duty of twenty-four per cent has increased to twenty-nine per cent; and twenty-nine per cent when figured on the pound at current rates of exchange instead of on $4.86} has become practically thirty-five per cent of a duty on dutiable goods coming into the country. This amounts in large degree to an embargo, so that my hon. friend is cut off from the revenue he expected.
What has happened? The Prime Minister two years ago guessed as to the amount of revenue he would receive from customs tariffs, and he guessed $22,000,000 wrong; he got $22,000,000 less than he expected. The Minister of Finance last year guessed $100,000,000 and he got $80,000,000. He was $20,000,000 out. But my hon. friend says that there is a favourable balance of trade. There was a small favourable balance of trade it is true but it was due-not to our selling more but- to our having to buy less. Imports totalled $442,000,060, only $42 per capita, the lowest since 1905. Our population is being starved for goods, which are necessary and desirable, in order that we may worship this god, the balance of trade. $442,000000 in imports as against $494,000,000 in exports! Our total trade is down nearly fifty per cent from 1931 and over sixty per cent from 1928. That is the trade record. What caused it? Duties were imposed in the special session and more in 1931. In his budget speech the Minister of Finance rather gave the impression that we had put on our tariffs after England had gone off the gold standard. Our tariffs were put on in May, 1931 while Britain did not go off gold, until September 1931. -Canada was one of those who started the parade, not one of those who came in after England had gone off the gold standard. Down went, imports and down went customs revenues, with the result that our customs revenue in 1931 was only $145,000,060 and for the eleven months of 1933, only $69,000,000. That shows the vicious circle and why my hon. friend is unable to get bis revenue. In the first place, we shut out the goods; in the second place
we cut off revenue, and in the third place, we shut in our own goods and then tax the man who can not sell his goods in order to make up what has been lost in customs duties. I think the Prime Minister gave the neatest possible example of that when he was discussing the imperial conference arrangements. This is something about which we happen to know down east. He is quoted on page 121 of Hansard as follows:
Under normal conditions Canada exports annually about 1,800 million board feet of lumber valued at $50,000,000, of which 1.445 million feet, valued at $39,000,000 has been going to the United States and 186 million feet valued at $6,474,000 to the United Kingdom. The recent United States import tax of $3 per 1,000 board feet has practically closed that market to Canada. New markets are essential. This applies to lower and common grades which comprise from 60 per cent to 70 per cent of the lumber sawn.
What caused the United States to put on that $3 per thousand board feet tax? The Bennett tariff of 1931. There was a retaliatory measure of $3 per thousand feet and then another $1 per thousand feet was added. My hon. friend had to bring a conference over from Great Britain in order to see if we could not sell them the 1,445 million feet which we lost in the United States because of the tariffs put on by my hon. friends in 1931. That is *how high tariffs work out, that is the result
The Budget-Mr. Ralston

of the red-blooded policy of my hon. friend the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion).
If my right hon. friend has learned anything, I think he has learned from the difficulties which have presented themselves in connection with markets. We are trying to find revenue and at the same time endeavouring to find markets. Here is what my right bon. friend predicted when he spoke in Vancouver :
If Mr. Mackenzie King thinks I will not so build up our agricultural and industrial life that its strength will drive our products into the markets of the world, then he is wrong. For that I will do. If he thinks I will not establish new markets for these products, strive with all my heart to retain them, drive our products with all my power into new markets, into old markets, into reluctant markets, he is wrong. For this I will do.
I am sure that when the Minister of Finance counts up the amount of duties received from the customs tariffs he will wish that the Prime Minister had used some other kind of dynamite than that which he has used for the purpose of forcing Canadian goods into these markets. He is now seeking frantically to make up the revenues which he has lost from customs duties by imposing a duty on sugar and by depriving pensioners of their pension. He is trying to make up what legitimate trade would produce. After all, the remedies are simple- cut your expenditures and increase your trade. This matter of a trade policy which will increase foreign trade, while I know it is not as new as some of the policies being advocated these days, is I think vital. Speaking in Winnipeg, in 1930 the Prime Minister told us where he got his trade policy. He said:
The. United States learned a long time ago that to become a great nation it must first look to itself. It therefore began to build up . its home market by keeping out of it the goods of other' nations. There was a time if when foreign countries had had their way, they could have smashed its youthful industries, dried up its revenue, wrecked its transportation systems and left it a country of idle workmen, of starving agriculturists, of futile manufacturers. Look at it now, marching to the slogan of America first.
If my right hon. friend willl read the evidence of Mr. Frank H. Simon given before the United States Senate committee only a few weeks ago, he will find that that slogan of America first is regairded as a rather dangerous one. I suppose my right hon. friend got the idea of Canada first from the idea of America marching to the slogan of America first. I think it will be found that the buy British policy has also been found to be one of doubtful utility. People are beginning to realize the truth of what appeared in a Can-

adian publication just the other day. This article reads:
A realization that no nation can live unto itself alone and that a spirit of international economic cooperation will usher in a return to more normal business conditions is steadily gaining ground.
Signed "Arthur Meighen". That article appeared in the Financial Post of November 5.
As my hon. friends apparently are not convinced, as we shall endeavour to keep on preaching the gospel to them, I may perhaps have to traverse some old ground. I want to point out that this slogan of Canada first, this raising of tariffs, has not attained that end to which my right hon. friend referred in Winnipeg as being the great objective of the American people and that which he desired to attain by his tariff policy. Let us see if it has developed production in our industries to supply the home market which my right hon. friend set such store by. I give just a very few figures:

Do we need any figures to-day to prove that there is unemployment in Canada; that unemployment has not been ended? The figure of 800,000' unemployed has been mentioned, and it has been stated that $123,000,000 has been spent on relief. The Prime Minister, when he came to the house in 1930, said that as regards curing unemployment, if the measures which he submitted were productive of the good which he indicated they hoped for, the number, which was 117,000, would steadily decrease and the maximum anticipated number of 177,000 would not be reached. Is there any doubt that the policy of high tariffs and economic isolation has failed?
This brings me to what I submit is the most serious defect in the whole budget. That is, that while it does not reduce expenditures, and while it imposes more taxation, it provides for nothing whatever in connection with the fundamental improvement of conditions in this country. Let me read a passage from the first part of the budget speech of the Minister of Finance. I feel that I ought to take the time of the house to put it on Hansard, because it is indicative of the attitude of my hon. friends opposite. He said:
There are those who decry the possibility of an international solution and who insist that we should seek remedies at home for present
conditions. I do not wish to minimize the difficulties and delays which are involved in any program based on international agreement, or to overlook the plain duty which rests upon every nation to keep its own house in order and to strive to the utmost by domestic action to accelerate the processes of business recovery. However, one cannot fail to observe that the present crisis is international, both in its causes and its effects, and that the remedy must be sought in international understanding and cooperation. Slowly, but nevertheless surely, the world is approaching full realization of the fact that the day of national selfsufficiency is past, that an international disease car, only be cured by an international remedy.
Therefore, I look forward hopefully to the World Economic and Monetary conference which is expected to meet in London in the near future, and to -which we propose to give our whole-hearted support. Members of this house have already had an opportunity of studying the agenda of that conference prepared by an able committee of experts. I am hopeful that on the basis of this agenda-
Note this:
-a program can be worked out for the relaxation of exchange controls and other excessive restrictions on international trade, for the stabilization of currencies and for the stimulation of a rise in the world level of wholesale prices. The success of this conference assumes a prior or simultaneous settlement of the war debt question and some appeasement of political fears and rivalries as a result of progress in disarmament discussions or otherwise. If these prerequisite conditions can be achieved, it Should be possible to reach agreement upon a program which would be effective in restoring world confidence and initiating an early recovery of business activity. The world has this solution within its grasp and in my opinion there is no other-short of prolonged and painful liquidation, if this indeed can be called a solution. Events are moving rapidly, driven by the urge of economic necessity. On this fact may rest the basis for a greater degree of optimism than has obtained in many months.
No self-reliance! No leadership! No courage! No suggestion of anything that we in this country may do, but we are leaning altogether on the world economic conference if, as or when there is one, and we are not even yet sure that there is to be one! If we can get a relaxation of exchange controls; if excessive restrictions on trade can be removed: if there can be a stabilization of currencies; if the world level of prices rises; then if prior to or simultaneous with this, there is a world debt settlement and if there is an appeasement of political fears and rivalries, we are on the road to economic recovery; otherwise liquidation.
I am reminded of the classic phrase of the Prime Minister because it has become a classic now: " Mr. King promises you conferences; I promise you work. Which plan do you like best?"
This is what Mr. Beaudry Leman, general manager of La Banque Rationale, has to say
337S
The Budget-Mr. Ralston

of the world economic conference, rather indicating that it is doubtful whether we are going to have definite action from that body. He said:
It would be difficult to conceive how any government would surrender to a body of representatives chosen from seventy nations the power to control its economic policies. One may hope, however, that the delegates to the conference may agree on some broad policy which would promote the economic recovery. The nations of the world depend upon one another to such an extent that agreements that are international in scope are necessary, but-
And I impress this on the Minister of Finance-*
-this necessity in no way absolves each country from establishing sound policies within its own boundaries.
That is where, it seems to me, the Minister of Finance completely falls down, if I may use the expression, in connection with this budget.
Reciprocity with the United States has been mentioned, and I refer to it now. The Prime Minister, in the debate on the resolution which was moved by the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff), had something to say about the matter. I think the bouse and the country have reason to congratulate the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough on having brought this resolution before the House of Commons. I want to point out that in connection with that as with other matters, this government is simply supine, listless, lethargic, and proposes to await the turn of events. Let me point out how my right hon. friend received this proposal. One would have thought it would provide some means for an extension of our trade. I have already mentioned with regard to the fishing industry the millions of dollars' worth of exports that we send to the United States, and that is our natural market for these products. In 1911 my right hon. friend the Prime Minister said:
One of the strongest reasons I had for opposing the reciprocity agreement was-
Not that it was an indefinite agreement, not that it could be changed at any time, but- -that it threw into the melting pot for solution a question that involved a problem of patriotism.
That is what he said in 1911, at page 23 of Hansard. In this house the other night he said:
On more than one occasion I have in this house indicated clearly the reasons I for one was opposed to that measure. First, it was an agreement incorporated into the statutes of both countries for that year, and it mentioned a limited number of items. But it was so

framed that the change by this dominion of its tariff with respect to any one of those items terminated the agreement; secondly, the agreement was for no period of time, or for no definite length of years.
A different reason from that which he gave in 1911, when reciprocity involved a question of patriotism,. But he said the other night that he earnestly desired some arrangement with the United States. What does he and the Minister of Finance propose to do about it? This a time when action is required. This is what my right hon. friend said the other night.
In my judgment all we can do is follow the course that has been followed by successive governments and indicate clearly our willingness to negotiate on terms that are fair and reasonable, to quote the words that have been used by both Liberal and Conservative prime ministers and ministers of finance. We can only be ready and willing to avail ourselves of any proposals that are fair and reasonable and are not of such a character as will involve injury to this country if they are speedily terminated.

speechtext:
The Budget-Mr. Ralston

time he goes to council and discusses the powers which the government has for fixing valuations for duty purposes. He said:
Furthermore, the tariff should be stable in its character, not subject to constant change and variation. Nothing is so harassing to a business or a financial man as to be constantly faced with the apprehension that overnight the tariff may be changed and large quantities of goods on hand or on order, seriously affected by such tariff changes. Nowadays a firm dare not issue a catalogue, for it does not know from hour to hour what tariff changes may be made. Tariff stability, voiced so eloquently by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding)-whom we miss so much from this debate-is what we require to-day.
If ever there was a government that had tariff instability, and if ever there was a government about which tariff instability is mbre firmly written on the records of the Department of National Revenue, the records of the importers of this country and the records of the consumers, I should like to know it. There has been absolute instability. There has been no chance in the world for people to know from day to day or even from hour to hour what the duty was going to be upon the goods with which they were dealing.
Mr. Speaker, I have taken longer than I expected to take, I have dealt with figures, a good many of them; I have dealt in some detail with a great number of the factors which affect our situation, and I want now to go back to plain, everyday fundamentals. Conditions of business in Canada, Incorporated, as I called it a few moments ago, are disturbing. By the end of the next fiscal year we will have added, since 1930, considerably over one 'half a billion dollars to the ' mortgage on the farm". We are not living within our income and, in fact are not trying to. We are deliberately planning to have at the end of the coming fiscal year- a deficit of nearly $100,000,000. We are pretending to reduce expenditures, but the way we are going about it is like chipping at the side of a mountain with a hand pick. The worst of all is that at the root of it our trade in basic commodities has dwindled to pitiful proportions, and yet we have the goods the world needs and must have. The government in one breath admits we ought to do something to help ourselves, but in the next it falls back supinely on the prospect of a world economic conference and, in the meantime, I submit with all due deference it is in a state of blue funk. The Prime Minister in a speech recently, referring to representations which had been made regarding a change of policy, asked "dare we do it?"

The other night in this house he made the declaration that the Canadian National Railways could be considered as being in receivership. Now we have the Minister of Finance suggesting that unless the world economic conference does something there will be nothing but liquidation. These are new words in respect of Canadian affairs, but their novelty does not make them any more welcome. The budget all the way through reflects this static, hopeless state of mind. It says "lop off a little expenditure, tax a great deal and wait until prosperity reaches us " instead of taking resolute measures to reach prosperity. I wish to protest against this static, fear-stricken attitude, but I bring the government this hope, not for itself-after the administration of the last two years it could hardly expect that-'but I do bring to this government from the people of Canada hope for the Dominion of Canada.
When the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance talk about receivership and liquidation I remind him that the people of Great Britain dared to risk the financial leadership of the world by going off the gold standard. I remind him that the people of the United States only a few weeks ago, despite the inconvenience and humiliation in connection therewith, turned the key in the door of every bank from Massachusetts to California and from the forty-ninth parallel to the gulf of Mexico; because they believed it was necessary so to do, they did it. These people dared to do these things because of the greater good which they hoped would come. I say to the Prime Minister-
